lesson.title: The Input Function: Letting the Program Listen Back
lesson.summary: input() pauses a running program, optionally displays a prompt, and waits for the user to type a response, always handing that response back as a string no matter what characters were typed.
lesson.body:
Where print() sends information out to the screen, input() is the built-in function that brings information back in from the person running the program. Calling name = input("What is your name? ") displays the prompt text, pauses execution completely, and waits until the user types something and presses enter. Whatever was typed is then stored in the variable name. If the user types Sam, the variable name now holds the string "Sam", and a line such as print(f"Hello, {name}!") building on F-String Formatting could greet them by name immediately afterward.

The single most important fact about input() is that it always returns a string, connecting directly to the String Type concept. This is true even if the user types digits. If a program asks age = input("Enter your age: ") and the user types 16, Python does not store the number 16; it stores the three-character string "16". This is easy to overlook because "16" looks identical to 16 when printed, but the two are different types underneath, and that difference has real consequences.

Trace what goes wrong without care: age = input("Enter your age: ") followed by next_year = age + 1 raises a TypeError, because Python will not add an integer to a string, the same restriction seen with string concatenation refusing to mix text and numbers. The fix is to convert explicitly with the built-in int() function: age = int(input("Enter your age: ")). Now trace it correctly. The user types 16, input() returns the string "16", and int() immediately converts that string into the integer 16, which gets stored in age. The expression age + 1 now works cleanly, evaluating to 17, because both operands are integers.

This design is intentional rather than an inconvenience. Input from a keyboard is fundamentally text, since a person could type letters, digits, or symbols, and Python has no way to know in advance which kind of value a given input call is meant to represent. Returning a string every single time keeps the behavior of input() perfectly consistent and forces the programmer to make an explicit, deliberate choice about how to interpret it, rather than having Python silently guess and risk guessing wrong.

One more failure mode is worth knowing about before it causes confusion. If the user does not type digits at all, say they type the word sixteen instead of 16, then int("sixteen") raises a ValueError, since Python cannot interpret those letters as a whole number. This is different from the TypeError seen earlier when a string and integer are mixed without conversion; a ValueError here means the conversion itself was attempted but the text simply did not represent a valid number. float() works the same way as int() for decimal input, converting a string like "9.5" into the number 9.5, and it will raise the same kind of ValueError on non-numeric text.

The pattern of prompting with input(), immediately converting the result with int() or float() when a number is expected, and then using that value in a calculation or an f-string is the basic skeleton of nearly every simple interactive Python program, and it depends on print(), input(), and string-to-number conversion all working together correctly.
